A sky-diver falls from a stationary balloon at time t = 0. As the sky-diver falls, her speed and the
air resistance increase until the force of the air resistance is equal to her weight.
Which graph best shows the variation with time t of the displacement s for the motion of the
sky-diver?
A
B
C
D

hints: Notice the sky-diver falls from a stationary balloon at $t = 0$, so initial velocity is zero and the $s$-$t$ graph must start with zero gradient.
Connect increasing speed to the gradient of displacement $s$ against time $t$, since gradient equals velocity $v$.
Use the final condition that air resistance equals weight to decide what the gradient must become when acceleration becomes zero at terminal velocity.
walkthrough: At $t = 0$ the sky-diver is stationary, so $v = 0$. On an $s$-$t$ graph the gradient is velocity, so the curve must start flat with zero gradient.

Initially weight is greater than air resistance, so there is a downward resultant force and downward acceleration. Velocity increases, so the $s$-$t$ gradient must increase and the curve steepens upward.
As speed increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force and acceleration decrease. The increase in velocity slows down, so the rate of steepening of the $s$-$t$ curve decreases.
Finally air resistance equals weight, resultant force is zero and acceleration is zero. The sky-diver reaches terminal velocity, which is constant.
Constant velocity means constant $s$-$t$ gradient, so the curve must finish as a straight line with positive slope.
Only the graph that starts flat, curves upward, then continues as a straight inclined line matches this history. This is option B.

A.explanation: Gradient keeps increasing, implying speed keeps increasing with no limit, so it never shows the constant terminal velocity when air resistance equals weight.

B.explanation: Starts with zero gradient for zero initial speed, steepens as speed increases, then becomes a straight line of constant gradient for terminal velocity.

C.explanation: Starts steep and flattens, implying large initial speed that decreases, which is opposite to a fall starting from rest with increasing speed.

D.explanation: Straight line from the origin implies constant velocity from $t = 0$, which ignores starting from rest and the period of acceleration.
